examples.problem:
The graph of the function $f(x),$ which is defined on $[1,6],$ is shown below. The areas of the regions between the graph and the $x$-axis are $5$ and $2,$ respectively (from left to right). Find the average value of $f(x)$ on $[1,6].$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013500/assets/6433d1ca57ceb334f304e894e2655ef50d987567fbcf219314302bb381fd9a83.png)
examples.worked_solution:
The average value of a function on a given interval is

$$
f_\textrm{avg} = \dfrac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

Here, we see that

$$
\int_{1}^{6} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x = -5 + 2 = -3.
$$

So, applying the average value formula, we find that the average value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6-1}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
The **exact** value of $c$ such that the average value of $f(x)=-15\sqrt{x}+6$ on the interval $[0,c]$ is equal to $-4$ is

$c=$
{{field-1}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
To solve for $c,$ we apply the average value formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ -4 & =\frac{1}{c-0}{\int }_{0}^{c}(-15\sqrt{x}+6)\,\text{d}x \\ -4 & ={\frac{1}{c}(-10{x}^{3/2}+6x)|}_{0}^{c} \\ -4 & =\frac{1}{c}[(-10{c}^{3/2}+6c)-0] \\ -4 & =-10\sqrt{c}+6 \\ -10 & =-10\sqrt{c} \\ 1 & =\sqrt{c} \\ c & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $c$ is 

$$
c=1.
$$
